content: 1. Avoiding behaviors such as sharing injection equipment is critical to reducing the risk of hepatitis C virus (HCV) transmission. 2. The reviewed studies did not assess potential undesirable outcomes, but the Guidelines Development Group acknowledged that individuals with HCV may face stigma, discrimination, and potential loss of employment and health benefits. 3. It is essential that HCV testing remains voluntary and that confidentiality is maintained to encourage testing uptake. 4. The Guidelines Development Group expressed concerns that individuals identified with HCV through enhanced screening in lowand middle-income countries might lack access to care and treatment. 5. Despite these concerns, the group emphasized the right of individuals to know their HCV status, as increased awareness could lead to greater demand for treatment. 6. The group concluded that the benefits of testing outweigh the potential harms. 7. The World Health Organization (WHO) is developing separate guidelines for hepatitis B and C screening and testing, which will address these issues in greater detail. 8. Targeted HCV testing linked to prevention and treatment services could reduce health disparities, particularly if conducted with cultural sensitivity, confidentiality, and linkage to care. 9. Transitioning from symptomatic testing to targeted screening of high-risk populations will require additional resources, including medical training, staffing, and equipment for phlebotomy, counseling, and serological screening. 10. Monitoring laboratory and clinical facilities is necessary to ensure high standards of practice. 11. Targeted testing costs vary by setting, and substantial screening efforts in high-prevalence populations may incur significant expenses. 12. The Guidelines Development Group stressed the importance of ensuring access to treatment following screening. 13. Infrastructure for both screening and treatment is necessary to improve outcomes such as quality of life and mortality, and resources for screening must be matched with resources for treatment. 14. Implementing these recommendations requires assessing the epidemiology of HCV in specific regions, which is challenging due to limited prevalence data in many countries. 15. In high-income countries, two approaches to expanding HCV testing include risk group identification and universal screening, though identifying risk groups is challenging due to stigma around behaviors like drug use. 16. Successful implementation requires a national HCV testing policy, adequate resources for test kits, healthcare worker training, and quality assurance programs. 17. Ensuring that diagnosed patients are referred for appropriate care, including therapy evaluation, lifestyle advice, and transmission prevention, is critical. 18. In the United States and Western Europe, all individuals with HIV infection should be screened for HCV upon enrollment in HIV care, with annual retesting for those at risk. 19. HCV infection rates are higher in individuals with HIV than in the general population, though rates vary widely by country. 20. There is a lack of direct evidence that HCV testing interventions improve treatment outcomes or reduce HCV-related morbidity and mortality, particularly in low-income settings. 21. Further research is needed to evaluate the long-term outcomes of HCV testing interventions and to develop novel, cost-effective laboratory techniques for confirming HCV infection. 22. Nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA is required to distinguish chronic HCV infection from resolved cases and is the standard of care for individuals who test positive for HCV antibodies. 23. Immediate NAT following a positive serological test is recommended to confirm chronic HCV infection, in addition to NAT as part of pre-treatment assessment. 24. The Guidelines Development Group emphasized that HCV testing should be voluntary, confidential, and linked to treatment referral for individuals with detectable HCV RNA. 25. Laboratories must operate within a quality-assurance framework to ensure accurate testing results. 26. Individuals with HIV/HCV coinfection may have false-negative HCV serological test results, and further research is needed to determine optimal CD4 count thresholds for NAT in these cases. 27. Behavioral interventions to reduce alcohol intake are recommended for individuals with HCV infection, as alcohol consumption accelerates liver disease progression. 28. The WHO ASSIST screening questionnaire can be used to assess alcohol intake levels and guide interventions. 29. Evidence suggests that alcohol reduction interventions can decrease alcohol consumption among individuals with moderate-to-high intake living with chronic HCV. 30. Although studies on alcohol reduction were conducted among HCV-uninfected individuals, the Guidelines Development Group believes the benefits are applicable to those with HCV infection.
